prompt:
Role and task instructions:
You are a helpful, respectful and honest assistant.

User request:
[Goal] Practice playing the instrument.
[Condition] You are unable to read sheet music
[Initial plan] Choose an Instrument > Learn Basic Terminology > Start with Simple Songs > Experiment with Melodies > Stay Consistent
[Problem] You find the plan quite vague and miss necessary steps.

For a given goal, make the plan more comprehensive and concrete. For each step you plan to take, mark with '[Step xx]'.
answer:
[Step 01] Choose one instrument.
Pick an instrument you enjoy hearing and can access regularly. Consider cost, noise, space, and comfort. Borrow or rent one if you are unsure, and commit to practicing it for the next four weeks.

[Step 02] Prepare your instrument and practice space.
Check that the instrument works, gather necessary accessories, and set up a comfortable seat or stand. For instruments that require tuning, use a tuner app and a beginner tuning tutorial.

[Step 03] Choose a learning method that does not require sheet music.
Find a beginner course that teaches through demonstrations, listening, and visible finger positions. Depending on your instrument, use keyboard diagrams, chord diagrams, tablature, or numbered finger guides. Learn how to interpret whichever guide you choose.

[Step 04] Learn essential terminology through examples.
Learn “pitch,” “note,” “beat,” “rhythm,” “tempo,” and “melody”; add “chord” if relevant. Listen to or play an example of each so that the words connect to sounds and actions.

[Step 05] Learn safe posture and basic technique.
Follow an instrument-specific demonstration for holding the instrument, positioning your hands, and producing sound. Practice for five minutes with relaxed shoulders and minimal tension. Stop and adjust if playing causes pain.

[Step 06] Practice producing a few clear notes.
Learn three to five notes or playing positions. Play each slowly several times, aiming for a clean, controlled sound. Use a visual guide until you can find them without repeatedly checking it.

[Step 07] Establish a steady beat.
Set a metronome to a comfortable speed, such as 60 beats per minute. Clap or tap once per click for 30 seconds, then play one familiar note per click. Next, alternate between playing and resting for one beat.

[Step 08] Select a suitable first song.
Choose a familiar melody with a short, repetitive section and few notes, such as “Hot Cross Buns.” Find a demonstration suited to your instrument that shows the playing positions without relying on sheet music.

[Step 09] Learn the song in small sections.
Listen to one short phrase, hum it, watch the demonstration, and copy it slowly. Repeat until you can play it correctly three times at an easy pace. Learn the next phrase, then connect the two.

[Step 10] Build a complete, steady performance.
Link the sections together at a speed you can control. Practice difficult transitions separately. Once you can play the whole melody comfortably, increase the tempo slightly; slow down again if accuracy deteriorates.

[Step 11] Practice learning by ear.
Spend three minutes finding a short, familiar tune without a tutorial. Sing its first few notes, locate the starting note, and test whether the next note sounds higher, lower, or the same. Check your attempt against a recording.

[Step 12] Experiment with your own melodies.
Use the three to five notes you already know to create a short musical phrase. Repeat it, change its rhythm, or alter its final note. Record one idea you like so you can play it again.

[Step 13] Follow a repeatable practice routine.
Practice for about 20 minutes on five days each week:

- 3 minutes: setup and relaxed warm-up.
- 4 minutes: clear notes and steady rhythm.
- 8 minutes: your current song, especially difficult sections.
- 3 minutes: learning by ear or improvising.
- 2 minutes: record a short attempt and note tomorrow’s focus.

[Step 14] Review progress and choose the next challenge.
Once a week, compare recordings and identify one improvement and one difficulty. Seek feedback from a teacher or experienced player when possible. When your first song feels comfortable, choose another that adds just one new skill, such as a new note, chord, or rhythm.
